stories.headline: CORE PCE JUMPS TO 3.3% YoY, HOTTEST SINCE LATE 2023, CEMENTING FED'S DEC. 9 HIKE PATH
stories.body: October core PCE rose 3.3% year-over-year and about 0.29% month-over-month, running slightly above the roughly 3.2% consensus, while headline PCE rose 3.8% YoY and 0.3% MoM, in line with forecasts; the hot core print all but locks in a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December 9 meeting with the funds rate at 3.75%-4.00%.
stories.explain: Core PCE strips out food and energy and leans heavily on housing and healthcare services, so a reading at its hottest since late 2023 signals price pressure is broadening beyond categories the Fed can dismiss as noise. Futures had already been pricing roughly 75-80% odds of a December hike, and a print this hot removes the committee's last realistic excuse to hold, which is why it moved stocks and yields almost immediately on release.

stories.headline: DOW RECOVERS TO CLOSE AT 50,183 WHILE S&P, NASDAQ SLIP AS NVIDIA SWINGS FROM -8% TO -4%
stories.body: The Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an early drop of more than 1% to close up 0.33% at 50,182.95, while the S&P 500 fell 0.25% to 7,182.78 and the Nasdaq 100 dropped roughly 0.65%, after Nvidia tumbled as much as 8% intraday on the hot PCE print before paring losses to close down about 4%.
stories.explain: The hot core PCE reading pushed Treasury yields higher intraday, raising the discount rate applied to the far-out cash flows AI and chip stocks are priced on, which is exactly why Nvidia and its peers took the brunt of the selloff. Light, pre-Thanksgiving trading volume then let the Dow's less rate-sensitive, price-weighted components pull that index back to a gain even as the broader, cap-weighted market finished lower.

stories.headline: AI-LED SELLOFF DEEPENS: NASDAQ COMPOSITE DOWN NEARLY 10% IN NOVEMBER AS RATE PATH REPRICES GROWTH STOCKS
stories.body: Beyond today's single-day moves, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite has slid almost 10% in November as a string of hotter-than-expected inflation prints and fading rate-cut odds forced investors to reprice the long-duration AI and chip stocks that ran up sharply during 2025's AI-capex boom.
stories.explain: Growth and AI stocks derive most of their valuation from cash flows far in the future, so their prices are unusually sensitive to the discount rate used to value those flows; when yields rise because the market pushes out rate cuts or, as today, prices in a hike, the present value of those distant profits falls disproportionately versus a value stock earning steady cash now. November's near-10% Nasdaq Composite decline is the clearest evidence that this rate-sensitivity channel, not a change in AI fundamentals, has driven most of the month's losses.

stories.headline: OIL JUMPS 4.2% TO $84 AND GOLD RISES TO $3,618 AS THE DOLLAR SLIDES ON RATE-PATH UNCERTAINTY
stories.body: WTI crude rose 4.24% to around $84 a barrel and gold climbed 1.94% to roughly $3,618 an ounce, even as the dollar index slipped 0.28% to 103.71 — a combination that broke from the usual pattern of a higher-for-longer Fed outlook pressuring both oil and gold at once.
stories.explain: Oil's jump looks driven by supply-side risk rather than the macro data, since crude can rally even as a hot inflation print would normally argue for tighter policy and a stronger dollar; that divergence shows up when a real, barrels-off-the-market shock overwhelms the usual rate-and-dollar arithmetic. Gold rising alongside a softer dollar is the more textbook move, since gold is dollar-denominated and gets cheaper for foreign buyers when the DXY falls, but gold climbing together with a hot inflation print also reflects investors leaning on it as an inflation hedge heading into the Fed's December 9 decision.

stories.headline: HUANG'S DEC. 1 CLOSED-DOOR TESTIMONY LOOMS AS KEY RISK EVENT LAYERED ON TOP OF THE FED DECISION
stories.body: With Nvidia shares whipsawing between an 8% intraday drop and a 4% close, markets are increasingly focused on former CEO Jensen Huang's December 1 closed-door testimony before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China select committees over his alleged ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, with general counsel Tim Teter following on December 2.
stories.explain: A transcribed, closed-door congressional interview on national-security grounds carries real legal and reputational risk distinct from ordinary earnings volatility, since lawmakers can compel detail on Nvidia's security protocols and China-exposure decisions the company has so far only addressed in statements. That makes December 1 a binary-feeling event for the stock sitting just eight days before the Fed's December 9 decision, which is part of why Nvidia's swings have been so outsized relative to the rest of the market this week.

deepDive.title: Why Black Friday Numbers Move Markets More Than You'd Think
content: Markets are closed today, but the data about to be generated at malls, warehouses, and checkout pages over the next four days will matter more to the Fed's December 9 decision than almost anything else on the calendar. Personal consumption expenditures make up roughly two-thirds of US GDP, and the holiday shopping window from Black Friday through Cyber Monday is the single densest stretch of consumer-spending data the economy produces all year. With core PCE just printing its hottest reading since late 2023, investors are watching Black Friday weekend not for retailer stock picks but as a real-time read on whether the American consumer is still spending through higher-for-longer rates or finally cracking under cumulative price pressure.

The mechanism runs through two channels at once. First, aggregate retail-sales figures feed directly into the GDP accounts the Fed uses to judge whether the economy is running hot enough to justify a hike; Adobe is projecting $275.1 billion in US online holiday sales this season, up 6.7% year-over-year, while Bain expects the four-day Black Friday-to-Cyber-Monday window alone to top $85 billion, growing faster than the holiday season overall. Second, individual retailers' same-store sales and margin commentary, reported over the following two weeks, tell the Fed and markets whether that spending came from income growth or from discounting and buy-now-pay-later financing — a distinction that determines whether strong headline sales represent healthy demand or a consumer stretching to keep up.

What most people miss is that resilient holiday spending can be bad news for stocks even though it sounds like good news for the economy. A consumer that keeps spending freely gives the Fed more room, not less, to follow through on the hike path the core PCE print just reinforced, because strong demand is itself inflationary pressure the committee has to lean against. The historical parallel is 2021 into early 2022, when blowout holiday sales coincided with the Fed's pivot from calling inflation "transitory" to launching the fastest hiking cycle in four decades — strong consumption data was a trigger for tightening, not a reason to relax it.

That is the lens to apply to this weekend's numbers heading into the blackout period before December 9. If Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales come in toward the strong end of Bain's and Adobe's forecasts, expect it to reinforce rather than ease the case for a hike, adding to pressure on the same long-duration, rate-sensitive AI and chip names that sold off hardest on Tuesday's PCE print. A softer-than-expected number, by contrast, would be the first real crack in the "resilient consumer" narrative that has kept the Fed comfortable raising rates into a historically strong economy, and it is exactly the kind of data point that could move the needle on a decision markets currently treat as a near lock.
